 RCP in the vicinity of $\nu=1$. The quenching of absorption to the  
 lower spin state is directly linked to an increase in the  
 absorption to the upper spin state. The calculated spin-polarization is  
 depicted as a function of filling factor $\nu$ utilizing the lowest energy  
 LCP transition for the spin-up occupancy and data from both the RCP  
 (solid line) and LCP (dashed line) transitions for the spin-down state  
 occupancy.

transitions (in LCP and RCP) to the ground Landau level are depicted as a  
function of magnetic field and compared to the computations. The  
transitions are specified in the lower left, and spectra and  
calculations at 12T are depicted versus energy in the upper insets. Note  
that while some discrepancy exists in the absolute energy position, the  
calculated matrix elements capture very closely the strength of the  
optical transitions.  

\noindent {\bf Illustration ~\ref{sky-fig3}:} The  calculated  
spin-polarization $S_z$ presented as a function of filling factor $\nu$  
for $1.4$ and $0.5$K. The solid line fit assumes a macroscopic spin of  
$\sim 3.7$ per flux quanta, while the dashed, dotted, and dash-dot fits  
assume a single particle self-consistent exchange-enhanced $g$-factor  
model with appropriate ranges of broadening and temperature.  

\noindent {\bf Illustration ~\ref{sky-fig4}:} Spin-polarization as a function  
of temperature in sample A with a carrier density of $n=1.5\times  
10^11$cm$^-2$. The peak of the spin-polarization rises to $0.8$ for  
decreasing temperature where it saturates. Most remarkable is the increase  
in width of the region of spin-polarization, which may be due to a  
relatively wide $\nu=1$ integral Hall plateau in this sample, and the  
resultant effect of increased carrier localization on local exchange.

\section{Particulars of the numerical discretization}  
The system is digitized onto a square three-dimensional grid  
$L\times L\times L$  
with isotropic mesh spacing  
$h$  
and periodic boundary conditions enforced in all directions. Every location  
$i$  
has the phases  
$\theta_i^{(1)}$, $\theta_i^{(2)}  
and the three components $A_{ix}$, $A_{iy}$ and $A_{iz}$ of the vector $(\mathbf{A})_i$.  
The phase gradients are digitized by the finite difference estimation  
$
[\nabla\theta\sp{(a)}]_{i\mu}
=(\theta^{(a)}_{i+\hat{\mu}}-\theta^{(a)}_{i})/h  
$  
with  
$\mu=x,y,z$,  
so that the kinetic energy density at site $i$ can be expressed  
$
\sum_\mu(\theta^{(a)}_{i+\hat{\mu}}  
-\theta^{(a)}_i+hA_{i\mu})^2/h\sp2  
$.  
The magnetic field energy density term at site $i$ is computed from the definition of a curl as an infinitesimal rotation. Using the notation $x'=y$, $y'=z$ and $z'=x$, we can express the rotation around the plaquette $P$ with corner in $i$, with area $h$ and normal $\hat{\mu}$ as  
$
((\nabla\times\mathbf{A})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{\mu}})_i\approx  
(h^{-2}\oint_{P}\mathbf{A}\cdot d\mathbf{r})_i=  
h^{-2}  
(hA_{i\mu'}+  
hA_{i+\hat{\mu}',\mu''}  
-hA_{i+\hat{\mu}'',\mu'}  
-hA_{i\mu''})  
$. Denoting  
$
A_{i\mu'}+  
A_{i+\hat{\mu}',\mu''}  
-A_{i+\hat{\mu}'',\mu'}  
-A_{i\mu''}  
=  
[\Delta\times\mathbf{A}]_{i\mu}  
$  
we obtain  
$
\lambda^2\left((\nabla\times\mathbf{A})^2\right)_i  
=\lambda^2\sum_\mu  
((\nabla\times\mathbf{A})\cdot\hat{\mathbf{\mu}})_i^2=  
(\lambda/h)^2\sum_\mu[\Delta\times h\mathbf{A}]_{i\mu}^2/h\sp2.  
$ We may furthermore reformulate the Josephson term as  
$
\xi_J^{-2}\cos(\theta^{(1)}-\theta^{(2)})  
=(h/\xi_J)^2\cos(\theta^{(1)}-\theta^{(2)})/h\sp2  
$.  

Since all terms in the Hamiltonian contain the factor $1/h\sp2$, both length scales appear in the units of $h$, and we can absorb $h$ into $\mathbf{A}$, we may set $h=1$ without loss of generality. After reformulating the kinetic energy terms into cosine $XY$-terms ($\cos(x)\approx1-x\sp2/2$) we acquire the Hamiltonian \eqref{eq:Hamiltonian}.

\section{Appendix A: Coupling strength and its reliance on the sphere position}

The overlapping factor $\eta$ in Eq.\,(2) in
the main text can be clearly expressed as:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eta}
\eta^{2}=\frac{(\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\overrightarrow{e_{x}})^{2}+(\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\overrightarrow{e_{y}})^{2}}{\mathrm{max}\{|\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}\}},
\end{equation}
\noindent where
$\mathrm{max}\{|\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})|^{2}\}$
is the utmost magnetic field strength of the
cavity mode, and $\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})$
is the magnetic field magnitude at the location
$\mathbf{r}$ of the YIG sphere,
$\overrightarrow{e_{j}}$ with $j=x,y,z$ are unit
vectors and $\overrightarrow{e_{z}}$ is along the
bias field orientation. In our experiment, the YIG
sphere is affixed to the cavity wall and moved
only along the $x$ orientation ($x_{max}=21.5$ mm
at the cavity boundary), as shown in the inset of
Fig.\,\ref{fig:position}(c). Due to the
$x$-dependent spatial arrangement of the ac
magnetic field within the microwave cavity, the
coupling strength between the magnon and the
microwave photon ($g\propto\eta$) can be modified
by placing the YIG sphere at different location
$x$. In addition, the fields near the wall are
polarized along $x$-orientation, thus we have
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:eta_approx}
\eta\approx\frac{\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\overrightarrow{e_{x}}}{\mathrm{max}\{\overrightarrow{h}(\mathbf{r})\cdot\overrightarrow{e_{x}}\}}.
\end{equation}


Figure\,\ref{fig:position}(a) displays the
reflection spectra at various location $x$ as a
function of frequency and the bias magnetic
field. The gap of the avoid crossing becomes
smaller as we shift the YIG sphere away from the
magnetic field apex ($x=0$). The spectra at
zero detuning magnetic field, where the magnon is
on resonance with the microwave photon, is
depicted in Fig.\,\ref{fig:position}(b). From
these spectra, the coupling strength is derived
as the half of the frequency separation.
Figure\,\ref{fig:position}(c) shows the derived
coupling strength as a function of $x$ (red
squares), and is in good accordance to the
distribution of the microwave magnetic field
(obtained by numerical simulation using COMSOL
3.5) according to Eq.\,(\ref{eq:eta_approx})
(solid blue line).

\begin{figure}[htpb]
\begin{centering}
\includegraphics[width=1\linewidth]{SC_FigS1_arXiv.eps} \caption{(Color online). (a) Reflection spectra at various locations as a
function of frequency and bias magnetic field.
(b) Reflection spectra at zero detuning magnetic
as the sphere is shifted away from the center. (c)
Coupling strength (measured, red squares) and
microwave field magnitude (simulated, solid blue
line) as a function of
location.}\label{fig:position}
\end{centering}
\end{figure}



\section{Appendix B: Linewidth manipulation}

In order to attain different coupling regimes, the
linewidths of both the microwave and the magnon
cavities are modified. The highest quality ($Q$)
factors for both cavities are defined by the
absorption of the material, thus it is
impractical to further enhance them. To
modify the $Q$ factor of the microwave resonance,
we use a piece of microwave absorber to increase
the absorption loss. To modify the $Q$ factor of
the magnon, iron filings are attached on the YIG
sphere surface to increase the absorption and
scattering losses. In both scenarios, the $Q$ factors
can be altered from the intrinsic value (several
thousands) to below 100, allowing us to explore
different coupling regimes.

\section{Derivation of formula~\eqref{normal-modes-eq}}
\label{App}
Here we derive the Formula~\eqref{normal-modes-eq} of the primary text.
In the parametrization \eqref{leading}, the left hand side of Formula~\eqref{NS-eq} takes the shape, 
\begin{align}\label{LHS
\rho(\partial_t v+v\partial_zv) \approx \rho_0 \ddot{\phi}\, .
\end{align}
To linearize the right hand side of Formula~\eqref{NS-eq} we note that the pressure is determined by the density via the relation of state such that 
\begin{align
P(z,t) = P[\rho(z,t)] \approx P[\rho_0(z)] - v_s^2[\rho_0(z)] (\rho_0 \phi)'\, ,
\end{align}
where the velocity $v_s$ is defined in Formula~\eqref{v_s}.
At equilibrium, Formula~\eqref{NS-eq} yields 
\begin{align}\label{cond
v_s^2 \rho_0' = -\rho_0 U'
\end{align}
We have therefore,
\begin{align
-P'-\rho U' \approx 
[ v_s^2 (\rho_0 \phi)']' +
(\rho_0 \phi)' U'
 \end{align}
Writing $(\rho_0 \phi)' U' =[ \rho_0 \phi U']' - \rho_0 \phi U''$ and using \eqref{cond} we obtain,
\begin{align
-P'-\rho U' \approx 
[ v_s^2 \rho_0 \phi ']' 
- (\rho_0 \phi) U''
 \end{align}
Writing 
\begin{align*}
[ v_s^2 \rho_0 \phi ']'  =\rho_0 [ v_s^2 \phi ']' +  \rho_0' [ v_s^2 \phi ']
\end{align*}
and using \eqref{cond} again we obtain
\begin{align}\label{first
-P'-\rho U' \approx 
\rho_0 [ v_s^2 \phi ']' -  
\rho_0 \phi ' U'
- \rho_0 \phi U''\, .
 \end{align}
The third, viscosity element on the right hand side of Formula~\eqref{NS-eq} reads
\begin{align}\label{third
\partial_z(\eta\partial_z v) = [\eta \dot{\phi}']'
\end{align}
Substituting Eqs.~\eqref{LHS}, \eqref{first} and \eqref{third} in Formula~\eqref{NS-eq} of the primary text we obtain
\begin{align
\ddot{\phi} = 
[ v_s^2 \phi ']' -  
 \phi ' U'
- \phi U'' + \rho_0^{-1} [\eta \dot{\phi}']'
\end{align}
For the solutions of the shape $\phi(z,t) = e^{i \omega t} \chi'(z)$ we obtain the formula,
\begin{align}\label{interim
 - \omega^2 \chi' = 
[ v_s^2 \chi'']' -  
\chi'' U'
- \chi' U'' +  (- i \omega)\rho_0^{-1} [\eta \chi'']'
\end{align}
Integration of Formula~\eqref{interim} over $z$ yields Formula~\eqref{normal-modes-eq}.

\end{appendix}

functions of 1D irreducible  
representations of the crystal point group. Therefore for a symmetry operation  
from this group $S_i$  

\begin{equation}  
\label{a1}  
S_i g\left({\bf k}\right)=g_i g\left({\bf k}\right)  
\end{equation}  

\noindent  
where $g_i$ is a quantity. Further, if there is a segment $P$ of FS  
which reproduces the entire Fermi sheet under the crystal group symmetry  
operations (FS=$\sum_i S_i P$) and  
the mean value of $g\left({\bf k}\right)$ over this segment of FS  
does not vanish, i.e. $\left<g\right>_P\neq 0$, then from the normalization  
$\left<g\right>=0$ and from the relation  

\begin{equation}  
\label{a2}  
\left<g\right>=\sum_i \left<S_i g\right>_P=\left<g\right>_P\sum_i g_i  
\end{equation}  

\noindent  
we obtain  

\begin{equation}  
\label{a3}  
\sum_i g_i=0  
\end{equation}  

\noindent  
Taking into account that $e^2\left({\bf k}\right)$  
is an identity representation for a real $e\left({\bf k}\right)$,  
which means that $S_i e^2\left({\bf k}\right)=e^2\left({\bf k}\right)$,  
we compute $\left<e^2g\right>$ as follows  

\begin{equation}  
\label{a4}  
\left<e^2g\right>=\sum_i\left<S_i\left(e^2g\right)\right>_P=  
\left<e^2g\right>_P\sum_i g_i  
\end{equation}  

\noindent  
Then Eqs. (A3) and (A4) yield $\left<e^2g\right>=0$.

of a s-wave component and a basis function $f\left({\bf k}\right)$ of a  
nonidentity 1D irreducible representation of the crystal point group, that is  

\begin{equation}  
\label{a5}  
e\left({\bf k}\right)=\left<e\right>+f\left({\bf k}\right)  
\end{equation}  

\noindent  
then $\left<eg\right>=\left<fg\right>$ and under the same assumptions  
about $g\left({\bf k}\right)$ we acquire  
$\left<e^2g\right>=2\left<e\right>\left<eg\right>$ which leads to a  
cancellation of the anisotropy of the scattering potential in  
$T_c$ equation (Eq. (\ref{e25})).  
We deduce from this, that in order to witness the effect of feeble  
anisotropic scattering, $e\left({\bf k}\right)$ and $g\left({\bf k}\right)$  
must belong to $A_{1g}$ representation with  
$g\left({\bf k}\right)$ normalized to satisfy $\left<g\right>=0$.

$g\left({\bf k}\right)$ transforms according to the symmetry of the  
crystal point group and are not valid  
in the instance of $g\left({\bf k}\right)$ characterized by a symmetry  
other than that of the crystal lattice.

In Schramm \& Kayser (1995) we introduced the intricate  
{\bf Beltrami Equation} as an suitable  
framework for the examination of arclets in cluster lensing. Corresponding real  
formulations have been created by Kaiser and Schneider \& Seitz (this volume,  
compare also the citations in Schramm \& Kayser 1995).  
Here, we demonstrate how the solutions of the  
Beltrami {\em differential\/} equation can be utilized to distinguish multiply imaged  
arclets.  
The Beltrami Equation  
\begin{equation}  
\frac{\partial w}{\partial \bar z}=\mu \frac{\partial w}{\partial z}  
\end{equation}  
states that a small ellipse in the deflector ($z=x+{\rm i} y$) plane given  
by $\mu $ is mapped locally by $w$ onto a circle in the source ($w=u+{\rm i} v$)  
plane.  
The axial ratio $\epsilon $ of the ellipse and  the direction angle $\varphi$  
are given by  
$\epsilon =(1-\left| \mu \right| )/(1+\left| \mu \right| )$ and  
$2\varphi=\pi +\arg (\mu )$, respectively.

We shall observe that the quasi-local energy $M$ is non-increasing 
in the untrapped area. The proof is entirely same as 
Hayward\cite{Ref:HAYI} and 
we shall express the metric in the double-null shape as 
\begin{equation}
ds^{2}=-2e^{-f}d\zeta_{+}\zeta_{-}+R^{2}(d\theta^{2} 
+\sin^{2}\theta d\varphi^{2}).
\end{equation}
The aforementioned shape is acquired by taking $\alpha=A=e^{-f/2}$ 
and $\zeta_{\pm}=(\eta \pm r)/\sqrt{2}$ in Eq.(2). 
Here we shall express the quasi-local energy as 
\begin{equation}
M(r,\eta)={1 \over 2}R\Bigl[1+{1 \over2}R^2 
\Bigl(e^{-f}\vartheta_{+}\vartheta_{-}-{2 \over 3}\Lambda 
\Bigr)\Bigr], 
\end{equation} 
where $\vartheta_{\pm}=2R^{-1}\partial_{\pm}R=e^{f/2}\rho_{\pm}$ 
and $\partial_{\pm}$ signifies the derivative with respect to 
$\zeta_{\pm}$. 
Without loss of generality, the components of the 
energy-momentum tensor in the spherically symmetric space-time is 
expressed as 
\begin{equation} 
T_{\pm\pm}=\psi_{\pm},~~T_{+-}=2\varepsilon~~ 
{\rm and}~~T_{\theta\theta}=T_{\varphi\varphi}/\sin^{2}\theta 
=R^{2}P. 
\end{equation} 
The Einstein equations Eq.(1) then become 
\begin{eqnarray} 
\partial_{\pm}\partial_{\pm}R+\partial_{\pm}f\partial_{\pm}R 
&=&-4\pi R\psi_{\pm}, \\ 
R\partial_{+}\partial_{-}R+\partial_{+}R\partial_{-}R 
+{1\over 2}e^{-f}&=&4\pi R^{2}\Bigl(\varepsilon+{1\over 8\pi} 
e^{-f}\Lambda\Bigr), \\ 
R \partial_{+} \partial_{-}f + 2\partial_{+} R \partial_{-} R 
+e^{-f} &=& 8\pi R^{2}(\varepsilon +e^{-f}P). 
\end{eqnarray} 
By utilizing the aforementioned equations, the derivatives of $M$ 
with respect to $\zeta_{\pm}$ are acquired as 
\begin{equation} 
\partial_{\pm}M=4\pi e^{f}R^{3}(\varepsilon\vartheta_{\pm} 
-\psi_{\pm}\vartheta_{\mp}). 
\end{equation} 

Here we assume that the matter fulfills the dominant energy 
condition, i.e., $\varepsilon \geq 0$ and $\psi_{\pm} \geq 0$. 
Then, from Eq.(A7), we determine that in the untrapped area 
$\vartheta_{+}>0$ and $\vartheta_{-}<0$, the 
quasi-local energy fulfills $\partial_{+}M \geq 0$ and 
$\partial_{-}M \leq 0$. 
If $z^{\mu}$ is outgoing spatial vector, the derivative 
of $M$ along this pathway is given by 
\begin{equation}
z^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}M=\beta_{+}\partial_{+}M-\beta_{-}\partial_{-}M, 
\end{equation} 
where $\beta_{\pm}$ are positive. Hence, in the 
untrapped area, $z^{\mu}\partial_{\mu}M \geq 0$ and 
this signifies that $M$ is non-increasing in any outgoing null 
or spatial direction in this area.

\section{The transfer function}

Our computation of the transfer function follows that of \cite{Larson:1999we}. To save space, we will only present the key measures here. The most significant difference is that we will include the contribution from both polarizations of the gravitational waves from the twin source. In this case, the total power on the laser interferometer is, instead of (21) in \cite{Larson:1999we},  
\begin{eqnarray}\brk{\Delta^2}&=&\int_0^{+\infty}\frac{dw}{2\pi}\,\frac{h_1^2T_1(w) +h_2^2T_2(w) -2h_1h_2T_3(w)}{(w\tau)^2}\,,\nonumber\\  
h_i&=&h_+(w)\cos2\tilde\phi_i+h_\times(w)\sin2\tilde\phi_i\,,\nonumber\\  
T_1&=&\mu_1^2\Big[1+\cos^2(w\tau)-2\cos(w\tau)\cos(\mu_1w\tau)\Big]\nonumber\\  
&&-2\mu_1\sin(w\tau)\sin(\mu_1w\tau)+\sin^2(w\tau)\,,\nonumber\\  
T_2&=&\mu_2^2\Big[1+\cos^2(w\tau)-2\cos(w\tau)\cos(\mu_2w\tau)\Big]\nonumber\\  
&&-2\mu_2\sin(w\tau)\sin(\mu_2w\tau)+\sin^2(w\tau)\,,\nonumber\\  
T_3&=&\mu_1\mu_2\Big[\cos(w\tau)-\cos(\mu_1w\tau)\Big]\Big[\cos(w\tau) -\cos(\mu_2w\tau)\Big]\nonumber\\  
&&+\Big[\sin(w\tau)-\mu_1\sin(\mu_1w\tau)\Big]\Big[\sin(w\tau) -\mu_2\sin(\mu_2w\tau)\Big]\,,
\label{def.delta2}\end{eqnarray}  
where $\mu_i=\cos\theta_i\,$. Note that the $i$'th laser link is at an angle $\theta_i$ with respect to $\hat{z}\,$, and at an angle $\tilde\phi_i$ with respect to $\hat{x}\,$; $c\,\tau$ is the arm length of the laser interferometer. More detail of the definition of $\brk{\Delta^2}$ can be found in \cite{Larson:1999we}.

As mentioned in the principal text, the control signal $\kappa$ is manipulated to $\arctan\kappa$ and $\sqrt{1+\kappa^2}$ by nonlinear electronic circuits.

\section{Characteristics of smooth cutoff functions}\label{app:cutoff}

In this Appendix we briefly survey the characteristics of compactly  
supported $C^\infty$ cutoff functions.  

Of fundamental utility in our derivations is a category of functions  
known as \emph{compactly supported $C^\infty$ bump functions}. These  
functions are defined so that their fourier transform  
$\widetilde{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)$ is compactly supported on the  
interval $[-\gamma, \gamma]$, and equal to $1$ on the middle third  
of the interval. Such functions satisfy the following derivative  
limits  
\begin{equation}\label{eq:chiderbound}  
\frac{d^j\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)}{d\omega^j} \lesssim  
\gamma^{-j},  
\end{equation}  
for all $j$ with the implicit constant depending on $j$. (If we have  
two quantities $A$ and $B$ then we use the notation $A\lesssim B$ to  
denote the estimate $A\le CB$ for some constant $C$ which only  
depends on unimportant quantities.) This is just about the best  
estimate feasible given Taylor's theorem with remainder and the  
constraints that $\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)$ is equal to $1$ at  
$\omega = 0$ and $\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)$ is compactly  
supported.  

The function $\chi_\gamma(t)$ has support throughout $\mathbb{R}$  
but it is dwindling rapidly. To see this consider  
\begin{equation}  
\chi_\gamma(t) = -\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \frac{1}{it}  
e^{-it\omega}\frac{d}{d\omega}\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega) d\omega  
\end{equation}  
which comes from integrating by portions. Continuing in this manner  
allows us to arrive at  
\begin{equation}  
\chi_\gamma(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}  
\left(-\frac{1}{it}\right)^j  
e^{-it\omega}\frac{d^j}{d\omega^j}\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)  
d\omega  
\end{equation}  
Since $\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)$ has all its derivatives  
restricted, according to (\ref{eq:chiderbound}), and using the compact  
support of $\widehat{\chi}_\gamma(\omega)$ we find  
\begin{equation}  
\begin{split}  
|\chi_\gamma(t)| &\lesssim \left|\int_{-\gamma}^{\gamma}  
\left(\frac{1}{it}\right)^j e^{-it\omega} \gamma^{-j} d\omega\right|  
\\  
&\lesssim \int_{0}^{\gamma} \frac{1}{|\gamma t|^j} d\omega \\  
&\lesssim \frac{1}{\gamma^{j-1}|t|^j},  
\end{split}  
\end{equation}  
for all $j\in \mathbb{N}$. Thus we find that $\chi_{\gamma}(t)$  
diminishes to $0$ faster than the inverse of any polynomial in $t$ with  
characteristic ``width'' $1/\gamma$. The existence and construction  
of such functions is discussed, for example, in \cite{vaaler:1981a,  
vaaler:1985a}.  


\end{document}

\section{Basic computation of constants}\label{sec:appendix}

For completeness, we provide a more basic derivation that the
stated constant is the correct normalization constant for the
Student $t$-distribution.


\begin{lem} We have \be 2\sqrt{\nu} \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{\nu-1} \theta d\theta
\ = \ \frac{\sqrt{\pi\nu}\
\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu}2\right)}{\Gamma\left(\frac{\nu+1}2\right)}.\ee
\end{lem}

\begin{proof} The assertion follows by induction; we sketch the main concept.
Assume we have demonstrated the assertion for all $\nu \le n$. Then \bea
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n+1}\theta d\theta & \ = \ & \int_0^{\pi/2} (1
- \sin^2\theta) \cos^{n-1}\theta d\theta \nonumber\\ & = &
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n-1} \theta d\theta - \int_0^{\pi/2} \sin
\theta \cdot \left(\cos^{n-1} \theta \sin \theta\right) d\theta.
\nonumber\ \eea We integrate the second term on the right by parts,
with $u = \sin \theta$ and $dv = \cos^{n-1} \theta \sin \theta
d\theta$. The $uv$ term vanishes at $0$ and $\pi/2$ and we are left
with \be \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n+1}\theta d\theta \ = \
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n-1} \theta d\theta - \frac1n \int_0^{\pi/2}
\cos^n\theta \cos\theta d\theta, \nonumber\ \ee which simplifies to
\be \int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n+1}\theta d\theta \ = \ \frac{n}{n+1}
\int_0^{\pi/2} \cos^{n-1}\theta d\theta. \nonumber\ \ee The assertion
now follows from standard properties of the Gamma function
($\Gamma(m+1) = m\Gamma(m)$ and $\Gamma(1/2) = \sqrt{\pi}$).
\end{proof}

\section{INTRODUCTION}  
\noindent  
Hadronic tau decays have been shown \cite{BNP} to be an  
effective laboratory for assessing perturbative and non-perturbative QCD. That is due both to the  
remarkable value of the tau mass located at a frontier regime between  
perturbative and non-perturbative QCD and to the outstanding quality of the ALEPH/OPAL \cite{ALEPH,OPAL} data. On the other hand, it is also known prior to the  
emergence of QCD, that the Weinberg \cite{WEINBERG} and DMO \cite{DMO} sum rules  
are crucial tools for managing the chiral and flavour symmetry realizations  
of QCD, which are disrupted by light quark mass terms to higher order \cite{FNR}  
and by higher dimensions QCD condensates \cite{SNWEIN} within the SVZ expansion  
\cite{SVZ}\footnote{For a review, see e.g. \cite{SNB}.}. \\ For accomplishing our program in the vector and $V+A$ channel~\cite{ZAKA1,ZAKA2,SNG,PICH2,TARRACH}, we  
investigate, in this document, the structure of the QCD vacuum using the ALEPH/OPAL data on the  
$V$-$A$ spectral functions in connection with a set of Laplace sum rules (LSR).  
We have already commenced the analysis of the $V-A$ channel in earlier papers \cite{SNL1,SNL2}. However, our  
primary motivation here is due to the recent interests on the  
$V-A$ hadronic correlator, which can serve as an order parameter of spontaneous chiral  
symmetry breaking in the chiral limit $m_q=0$. This correlator also controls the dynamics of the  
weak matrix elements of the electroweak Penguin-like operators \cite{ENJL,DONO}. These  
significant properties require a thorough structure of the associated QCD vacuum which can be  
characterized by the sum of power corrections \cite{SVZ}. A large number of papers on the  
estimations of these power corrections using different methods exist in the literature,  
but with conflicting results in \cite{ALEPH,OPAL,RAF04,PERIS,STERN,ZYA,IZ}  
and in  
\cite{PRADES,DOMINGUEZ,ROJO,MALT,CIULLI}. In the following we propose a set of Laplace transform sum  
rules (LSR) which can assist to clarify such discrepancies.  
We shall be concerned here with the $V$-$A$ two-point correlator:  
\begin{eqnarray}  
&\Pi_{\mu\nu}^{LR}(q)\equiv i\int d^4 x~ e^{iqx}\langle 0|{\cal T} J_\mu^L(x)\left(  
J_\nu^R(0)\right)^{\dagger}|0\rangle\nonumber\\  
&\stackrel{m_q\rightarrow 0}{=}-(g_{\mu\nu}q^2-q_\mu q_\nu)\Pi^{LR}(q^2)~,  
\end{eqnarray}  
built from the left-- and right--handed components of the local weak current:  
\begin{equation}  
J_\mu^{L}=\bar u\gamma_\mu(1-\gamma_5)d,~~~~~~~J_\mu^{R}=\bar  
u\gamma^\mu(1+\gamma_5)d~.  
\end{equation}  
Following SVZ \cite{SVZ}, the correlator can be approximated by:  
\begin{equation}  
\Pi^{LR}(Q^2)\simeq\sum_{d\geq 2}{{\cal O}_{2d}\over (Q^2)^d}  
\end{equation}  
where ${\cal O}_{2d}\equiv C_{2d}\langle{\cal O}_{2d}\rangle$ is the short hand-notation of the QCD non-perturbative  
condensates $\langle{\cal O}_{2d}\rangle$ of dimension  
$D\equiv 2d$ and its associated perturbative Wilson coefficient $C_{2d}$; $q^2\equiv -(Q^2 >0)$ is the momentum transfer.  
In the chiral limit $m_{u,d}=0$, there is no $D=2$ term as unflavored contribution of the renormalon-type  
\cite{ZAKA,ZAKA1,ZAKA2} vanishes. The spectral function $(v-a)$:  
\begin{equation}  
\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}\Pi^{LR}\equiv\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\left( v-a\right)~.  
\end{equation}  
has been measured by  
ALEPH and OPAL \cite{ALEPH,OPAL} using  
$\tau$-decay data. Within such a normalization, the original ``sacrosanct" first and second  
Weinberg sum rules \cite{WEINBERG,DMO} read, in the chiral limit $m_{u,d}=0$:  
\begin{eqnarray}  
{\cal S}_{0}&\equiv&\int_0^{\infty} dt ~\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}\Pi_{LR} -  
2f^2_\pi=0~,\nonumber\\  
{\cal S}_{1}&\equiv&\int_0^{\infty} dt ~t~\frac{1}{\pi}{\rm Im}\Pi_{LR} =  
0~,  
\end{eqnarray}  
where $f_\pi=(92.4\pm 0.26)$ MeV is the experimental pion decay  
constant.

\section{Introduction}\label{intro}  
All Lie algebras examined in this paper are finite-dimensional over the field $F$ and are soluble. The theory of saturated formations and of $\fF$-projectors was formulated in Barnes and Gastineau-Hills \cite{BGH}. The theory of $\fF$-normalisers was formulated in Stitzinger \cite{Stit}. The subsequent definition of intravariance for subalgebras of Lie algebras was provided in Barnes \cite{Frat}.

\begin{Definition} The subalgebra $U$ of the Lie algebra $L$ is said to be
{\em intravariant} in $L$ if every derivation of $L$ is expressible as the sum of an inner
derivation and a derivation which stabilises $U$. \end{Definition}

By \cite[Lemma 1.2]{Frat}, the intravariant subalgebras of $L$ are precisely those subalgebras $U$ with
the property that, if $L$ is an ideal of $L^*$, then $L^* = L + \sN_{L^*}(U)$. It was established in 
\cite[Theorem 2.2]{Frat} that, if $\fF$ is a saturated formation of soluble Lie algebras, then the
$\fF$-projectors of a soluble Lie algebra $L$ are intravariant in $L$. It seems logical to
conjecture that the $\fF$-normalisers also are intravariant. The following definitions are derived from
Stitzinger \cite{Stit}.

\begin{Definition} A maximal subalgebra $M$ of $L$ is called $\fF$-normal if it
complements an $\fF$-central chief factor of $L$. Equivalently, $M$ is
$\fF$-normal if for some chief factor $A/B$ of $L$, $M+A = L$ and the split
extension of $A/B$ by $M/\mathcal{C}_M(A/B)$ is in $\fF$. This is equivalent to
$L/\core(M) \in \fF$. $M$ is labeled $\fF$-abnormal if it is not $\fF$-normal, that
is, if $L/\core(M) \notin \fF$. \end{Definition}

\begin{Definition} A maximal subalgebra $M$ of $L$ is termed $\fF$-critical if $M$
is $\fF$-abnormal and $M + N(L) = L$ where $N(L)$ is the nil radical of $L$. \end{Definition}

\begin{Definition} A subalgebra $V \le L$ is termed an $\fF$-normaliser of $L$ if
$V \in \fF$ and there exists a chain of subalgebras
$$L = M_0 > M_1 > \ldots > M_n = V$$
with each $M_i$ $\fF$-critical in $M_{i-1}$. \end{Definition}

We shall need the following consequence of Stitzinger \cite{Stit}.

\begin{theorem} Let $U$ be an $\fF$-normaliser of $L$. Then $U$ covers every
$\fF$-central chief factor and avoids every $\fF$-eccentric chief factor of $L$.\end{theorem}

We now prove the asserted result.

\begin{theorem}\label{th-main} Let $\fF$ be a saturated formation. Let $L$ be a soluble Lie
algebra and let $U$ be an $\fF$-normaliser of $L$. Then $U$ is intravariant in $L$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof} Let $d$ be a derivation of $L$ and let $D = \langle d, L\rangle$ be the split extension of
$L$ by $d$. We must demonstrate that $\sN_D(U) + L = D$. We use induction over $\dim{L}$. Let $A
\subseteq L$ be a minimal ideal of $D$. Then $U+A/A$ is an $\fF$-normaliser of $L/A$, so by induction,
$\sN_D(U+A) + L = D$. Let $N = \sN_D(U+A)$. Since $A$ is an irreducible $D$-module and $L$ is an ideal
of $D$, all $L$-composition factors of $A$ are isomorphic, so either all are $\fF$-central and $U
\supset A$ or all are $\fF$-eccentric and $U \cap A = 0$. If $U \supset A$, the $\sN_D(U) = N$ and the
result holds. If $U \cap A = 0$, then $U$ is an $\fF$-projector of $U+A$ and is intravariant in $U+A$. 
As $U+A \triangleleft N$, we have $\sN_N(U) + (U+A) = N$ and $\sN_D(U) + L \subseteq  \sN_N(U) + (U+A) + L =
N+L = D$.
\end{proof}
